title: US Senator Attacks H-1B 'Ethnic Favouritism' as Indian Workers Describe Visa System as 'Permanent Anxiety'
excerpt: A US senator's broadside against India's 'visa temple' and H-1B workers coincides with mounting frustration among Indian professionals trapped in the lottery system
body:
A US senator has launched a sharp attack on what he called 'ethnic favouritism' in the H-1B visa programme, singling out Indian workers and the consular infrastructure that serves them. The remarks, which described Indian visa processing centres as a 'visa temple,' have reignited a politically charged debate over immigration policy that directly affects hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals in the United States.

The senator's comments come at a particularly raw moment for the Indian diaspora. On social media, a working professional who identified himself as an Indian tech worker shared a post that quickly went viral: after three consecutive failed H-1B lottery attempts, he described the visa anxiety as a 'permanent subscription' — a phrase that resonated across the community.

The H-1B programme, which grants 85,000 visas annually through a lottery system, has long been a flashpoint in American immigration politics. Indians consistently account for over 70 percent of H-1B approvals, a dominance that reflects both the depth of Indian talent in technology and the structural dependence of US tech firms on foreign workers. But that very dominance has made the programme a convenient political target.

For the estimated 300,000-plus Indian nationals currently in the H-1B backlog — many of whom have lived and worked in the US for a decade or more — the senator's remarks are more than political theatre. They represent a hardening of rhetoric that could translate into legislative action. Several bills in Congress seek to impose per-country caps, diversity requirements, or wage-floor increases that would disproportionately affect Indian applicants.

The diaspora's frustration is compounded by the green card backlog, which for Indian nationals now stretches beyond 50 years for employment-based categories. Workers who entered the system in their twenties face the prospect of retiring before receiving permanent residency — a limbo that affects career mobility, home ownership, and family planning.

Immigration attorneys note that the political environment has shifted markedly. 'Five years ago, the debate was about reform. Now it is about restriction,' said one Washington-based immigration lawyer who works primarily with Indian clients. 'The language of ethnic favouritism is designed to pit communities against each other, and Indian workers are the most visible target.'

For NRIs watching from India, the UK, Canada, and the Gulf, the American H-1B debate carries broader implications. It signals a tightening of the global welcome mat for skilled Indian workers — a trend visible in Canada's recent cap on international students and the UK's rising salary thresholds for work visas. The era of relatively frictionless skilled migration may be drawing to a close.
nri_angle: Directly impacts the largest segment of H-1B holders and their families; the green card backlog affects career and life planning for hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals in the US
